title: prinz (@deredleritt3r)
summary:
Most lawyers have no idea how to correctly use AI, and so the takes from lawyers on using AI for legal work are either overly pessimistic or overly optimistic.
The optimists don't realize that ~5% of the citations confidently generated by AI are hallucinations, and are in for a rude awakening.
The pessimists try to use AI as a blunt tool for all legal tasks, which naturally leads to subpar results.
The correct way to use current AI models for legal work is as a bespoke tool. Don't ask AI to generate a complex legal document de novo. But do ask AI to see if it can find examples of a bespoke provision that you've never encountered before. Don't ask AI to find all 100+ cases that hold X. But do ask AI to do "needle in the haystack" research for you - it sometimes finds needles FAST.
The key is to apply AI as leverage in those places that minimize the current models' shortcomings. Do this successfully, and your productivity as a lawyer will increase substantially.
Quoting @alexolegimas
I sent this to a friend, who is a partner at a prominent law firm. Their response, verbatim:
“lol no.
We’ve tried all the frontier models.
It’s useful for doing a first pass on low level stuff, but makes tons of mistakes and associate has to check everything.”

Quoting @Hangsiin
Insights from the OpenAI IMO Gold Medal Team Podcast
(@alexwei_ , @polynoamial, @SherylHsu02)
1. Their dedicated effort towards this year’s IMO lasted only about two months, which was a very short preparation period.
2. The core team consisted of just three members. (Of course, other teams provided some assistance as well.) Most of the work was led by Alex, with Noam and Sheryl contributing when the IMO date drew closer.
3. Regarding the readability of the model’s proofs, they considered uploading a more readable version on GitHub through ChatGPT but decided to publish the original version for transparency. They mentioned that they are fully aware of how to make the proofs more readable using ChatGPT.
4. For problem 6, they emphasized the significance of the model’s ability to output “no answer,” thereby avoiding hallucinations.
5. As for the Millennium Problems, they pointed out that these are extremely difficult problems with almost no progress even after a lifetime of work by many scholars. From a thinking-time perspective, solving such problems would require extending the current 1.5-hour thinking time for IMO problems by a factor of 1,000 or more, indicating that there is still a long way to go.
6. Noam mentioned that a major bottleneck in extending thinking time is evaluation: if thinking time is extended to 1,500 hours, evaluation would also take that long, creating a significant bottleneck.
7. Noam revealed that a multi-agent component was used in this IMO project, and it was employed to scale parallel computing. However, he stated that they cannot disclose the specific implementation details.
8. When asked about Putnam problems, Alex said that their model actually performs better on Putnam problems than on IMO problems. He added that future unexplored frontiers lie not in time-constrained competitions, but in problems that require longer and deeper reasoning.
9. When asked whether he agreed with Demis Hassabis’s statement that “the hardest part is creating interesting problems,” Noam said he agreed to some extent. However, he emphasized that the current pace of progress is incredibly fast and that there have always been hurdles for language model development. He stated that the next hurdle will be “How can we make the model come up with new questions?” and that he sees no barrier preventing them from achieving that goal.
10. Their approach is not focused on “making the model good at math” but rather on “developing general-purpose technology.” They said the technology used this time was a relatively new approach, developed recently. Their next step is to broadly integrate this technology into other OpenAI models to enhance overall reasoning ability, but it will take some time before it can be deployed worldwide.

title: prinz (@deredleritt3r)
summary:
Dario Amodei: "Continual learning is not as difficult as it may seem." 👀
Quoting @Hangsiin
Dario Amodei(@DarioAmodei) counters the criticism that the lack of continual learning is a fundamental limitation of LLMs with a three-part argument:
1. The Potential of LLMs is Immense, Even Without Solving Continual Learning.
-It's like having 10 million Nobel laureates who can no longer learn new information. With their existing static intelligence alone, they could still achieve countless biological breakthroughs.
-With just their current capabilities, LLMs are transformative enough to impact the entire economy, and people are underestimating this. Their value is immense, even when you factor out the ability for continual learning.
2. The 'Context Window' Serves as a Practical Form of Short-Term Learning.
-As a conversation progresses within a long context window, the model absorbs and reacts to new information, which functions as a type of real-time learning. While the model's underlying weights don't change, it can understands and utilizes the context of the conversation.
-The current bottleneck is not the technology to expand context length itself, but the challenge of inference support to serve it efficiently. In theory, it's already possible to expand the context to the amount of information a human hears in a lifetime (approx. 100 million words).
3. Continual Learning is a Solvable Technical Challenge, Much Like the "Reasoning" Problem of the Past.
-Approaches like RL or the 'inner-outer loop' structures could enable long-term learning by directly updating the model's weights.
-Just two years ago, reasoning was seen as a fundamental limitation of LLMs, but it was ultimately solved by techniques like RL. He suggests that continual learning is a similar type of problem that will likely be overcome by a combination of "scale and a slightly different way of thinking."
-Without getting into specifics, he adds that there is already some evidence to suggest this problem is not as difficult as it may seem.

OpenAI's "universal Verifier": the tl;dr
via The Information
-OpenAI is developing “Universal Verifier,” a new AI system for automated quality control in reinforcement learning—crucial for the further development of GPT-5.
-The goal: to reliably evaluate difficult answers, for example in mathematics or creative texts, where right and wrong are not easily measurable objectively.
-The Verifier uses an LLM to check other models, similar to GANs: one model generates, the other controls.
-Practical example: In mathematical proofs, the Verifier checks not only the final result, but every single logical step.
-Performance test passed: A GPT model using this approach won a gold medal at the International Mathematical Olympiad.
-According to OpenAI researcher Noam Brown, this also improves LLMs in subjective areas such as creative writing or business decisions.
-Outlook: The Universal Verifier could open the door to reliable AI in complex, human fields of thought – far beyond programming.

title: prinz (@deredleritt3r)
summary:
The OpenAI model that won gold on the IMO was a sidequest by 3 researchers to put together a checkpoint of whatever reasoning system OpenAI has internally over only ~2 months.
The same checkpoint (with light harnessing) then proceeded to also win gold on the IOI.
OpenAI's overall research direction is to get models to think for much longer time horizons than just an hour or two. More thinking = better reasoning, and we see this empirically with different versions of GPT-5 Thinking that are available at Plus and Pro tiers and via API.
So, does OpenAI have models that can think for even longer time horizons than the checkpoint that won IMO/IOI gold? Obviously yes. We know that the OpenAI model that won second place in the AtCoder competition ran autonomously for 10 hours(!), iterating on its previous reasoning to find better and better solutions to the problem.
The ability to iterate better and better solutions autonomously over a long time horizon is surprising, and seems to be mostly overlooked currently. We've heard Sam Altman say many times that he expects 2026 to be the year of novel scientific discoveries, and I wonder whether this is the path that gets us there.

title: prinz (@deredleritt3r)
summary:
New paper by BlackRock shows how a multi-agent team built on top of GPT-4o can help with stock analysis.
The team consists of:
- a Fundamental Agent, which engages in qualitative and quantitative analysis of financial disclosures (e.g., SEC filings)
- a Sentiment Agent, which reviews recent financial news
- a Valuation Agent, which values the stock using a valuation tool
Each of the agents comes up with its own conclusion based on its analysis. The agents then "debate" (i.e., each agent's analysis is updated based on results obtained from the other two agents). The debate continues until all three agents agree to either recommend "Buy" or "Sell".
The framework is scalable, and can be expanded to include other agents ("portfolio managers may benefit from a Technical Analysis Agent for short-term trend detection or a Macro Economist Agent focused on economic policy and macroeconomic data").
The study "demonstrat[es] that coordinated agent reasoning can enhance decision quality and mitigate human cognitive biases". "While not yet a full portfolio optimization engine, [this multi-agent system] represents a foundational step toward agentic investment systems."

The U.S. government's investment in Intel has "early-stage Manhattan Project" vibes.
First, the facts:
- The U.S. government has agreed to acquire just a hair under a controlling stake in Intel - 9.9%.
- The U.S. government does NOT get a Board seat or any other governance or information rights. In Intel's own words, it's "passive ownership".
- The U.S. government can vote its shares, but "agrees to vote with the Company’s Board of Directors"... WITH LIMITED EXCEPTIONS.
- We won't ever know what these "limited exceptions" are, but we definitely know why the U.S. government has purchased the stake in Intel. As part of the deal, the U.S. government has received an additional 5-year warrant exercisable at below current FMV ($20/share) for an additional 5% of Intel's shares. This warrant is exercisable "only if Intel ceases to own at least 51% of its foundry business".
In other words: "lose control of your foundry, and we take significant control of your business." (Note that it's not clear whether exercising the warrant would also make some of the "passive ownership" provisions go away - e.g., by providing the U.S. government a Board seat or enabling its shares to vote independently from the Intel Board.)
@SemiAnalysis_ put it best: "By taking a leadership stake, now it is clear how we make chips in the US again, and that is at Intel."

Quoting @huybery
I believe LLMs will inevitably surpass humans in coding.
Let us think about how humans actually learn to code. Human learning of coding has two stages. First comes memorization and imitation: learning syntax and copying good projects. Then comes trial and error: writing code, running it, fixing it, and improving through feedback.
These two stages map closely to how LLMs learn. Pretraining (PT) compresses the entire corpus of code into parameters far beyond any human capacity. Reinforcement learning (RL) aligns the model with execution through feedback, but at a speed and scale humans cannot match, with millions of rollouts completed in a short time. This advantage in parameter capacity and iteration means it is only a matter of time before models move ahead of humans.
More importantly, code is not only the foundation of human productivity but also the starting point of recursive improvement. When models can write and optimize their own code, what we see is no longer just AGI but the first signs of ASI. AI4AI is on the way.

title: prinz (@deredleritt3r)
summary:
There is no "how to use AI" rulebook for lawyers, and I cannot emphasize enough what a huge problem that is.
At my firm, we have been told that AI hallucinates, and lawyers therefore must always double-check its work. The rest is left up to the user to discover.
But it's not intuitive that, e.g., GPT-5 Pro can be used VERY effectively to find all statutes, regs and guidance in a state about Topic X, AND sometimes pulls in sources that even I would not have thought to check, BUT will sometimes miss one source or summarize something too vaguely. I know these boundaries quite well, and have been quite successful in leveraging ChatGPT in my legal work (and still learning how to do it even more effectively), but most other lawyers do not.
Go one level deeper, and you will find yet another problem: most lawyers - especially more senior lawyers - are extremely non-technical. My ability to manipulate spreadsheets at a decent level has at times been seen as voodoo by my colleagues throughout my legal career. And more senior people have work flows that "already work well", and are very reluctant to change them. Integrating AI into these existing work flows is possible - just like computers, e-mail, Zoom video calls, etc., were integrated into them in the past - but some appreciation of this kinds of friction is required in order for AI to truly become a widespread tool in the legal profession.
Quoting @willccbb
the people with the most useful domain expertise are not the weekend-warrior agent hackers or PhD dropouts. they're doctors and lawyers and accountants and bankers and professors. we need to teach them how to do this.

summary:
I've been thinking about what it means to say "there's more to being a good software engineer than just writing code" for my work (law).
Parsing where we are today vis-a-vis tasks that lawyers actually do:
- Legal research. AI is already great at this when the universe of sources is limited to maybe a few dozen documents. Need to be able to connect AI to Lexis/Westlaw to research case law. Increasing research run-time to 1 hour+ is probably necessary for this. Might still need smarter models than even GPT-5 Pro to increase accuracy of overall results after analyzing 100+ cases (could be wrong about this; GPT-5 Pro may already be good enough). Overall, feels like the next generation of models will get us there.
- Due diligence. Need an agentic workflow for diligence that goes through the entire data room (would probably take hours) and builds out a comprehensive diligence report with sources. Someone should be building this. This is the exact use case that the frontier AI labs tell you is a great business model (may be janky now; will suddenly work incredibly well with the next generation of models).
- Drafting/revising agreements. Need an agentic workflow that lets the user pick a template for the agreement or tell the model where to find precedent; connect to the diligence tool above to populate reps/covenants; iterate on the agreement section by section to account for the parties, transaction terms, user feedback. Someone should be building this. This is yet another huge opportunity (just like the diligence tool).
- Writing e-mails with advice/legal memos. E-mails are already solved; may need to instruct AI models to write in a better "legal voice". Memos are probably yet another agentic workflow. I think that a model that can draft an IMO proof should also be able to write a good legal memo.
Many other things lawyers do (legal briefs; court correspondence and filings; regulatory filings) will have similar workflows to those described above.
We need to solve hallucinations to increase the accuracy and reliability of all these tools.
Someone will eventually build a "Jeeves the Lawyer" app that can run these tasks in the background and output simple advice and legal documents for business people. Quick review by your one in-house "human lawyer in the loop", and you're done.
In this world, the role of human lawyers begins to be reduced to checking Jeeves; having phone negotiations with the counterparty (based mostly on whatever Jeeves told you was important to negotiate); in-person court appearances; working for the government (mostly a sinecure); business development.
3+ years later, even those roles might diminish or be completely gone.
The new world dawns.
Quoting @polynoamial

But this is happening at the exact same moment when it’s getting clearer what the future of AI agents are going to look like.
The type ahead or chat interaction paradigm of AI maxes out at double digit productivity gains because you’re inherently rate limited by how fast you can type or interact with the system. You’re still doing most of the work, and AI is just providing quick answers and suggestions to move you along faster.
The AI agent model, where you can run many agents in the background in parallel, actually can deliver multiples in productivity gains. Coding is where we’re seeing this first, but it will come for most categories of knowledge work.
The only trick is that it’s likely not as easy to adopt as the first paradigm was, because it requires a change in workflow. But those that get there are going to see the future faster, and get more compounding returns, than those that don’t.

A point I've heard both Carl and Gwern make is that with primates, evolution finally found both a scalable brain architecture AND a niche that rewarded marginal increases in intelligence.
Some birds are really smart for the size of the brains. But they're in a niche that punishes bigger heavier brains - they'll fall out of the sky.
The difference in neuron count between primate species' brains is proportionally to their brain mass, suggesting a scalable brain architecture, By contrast, for rodents and insectivores, neuron count scales sublinearly with mass.
Another feedback loop like the cooking example: opposable thumbs allow us to make tools, which increases the value of having bigger brains to design said tools. Which incentivizes more dexterous hands...

As a neurosurgeon I care a lot about road safety.
By now you’ve probably seen @Waymo’s stunning safety results (like 91% fewer serious crashes). But they didn’t just publish data headlines. They released the raw CSV files and data dictionaries.
I did a much deeper analysis. A fascinating story emerges when you analyze how they’re achieving this.
This isn’t incremental improvement - it’s categorical. We’re looking at the potential elimination of traffic deaths as a leading cause of mortality.
The intersection breakthrough: Waymo has essentially solved intersection crashes, with 95% fewer injury incidents than human drivers in the same locations. That’s transforming the deadliest driving scenario.
The national math: If every US vehicle performed like Waymo, we’d prevent 33,000-39,000 deaths annually and save $0.9-1.25 trillion in societal costs. Even partial adoption at 27% would save ~10,000 lives per year. In terms of magnitude, this would be the equivalent of eliminating every pedestrian death nationally in a year.
The physics signature: Here’s what fascinates me: 47% of Waymo’s contacts involve less than 1 mph delta-V. They’re not just avoiding crashes; they’re converting unavoidable incidents into gentle bumps. It’s like having physics itself on your side.
We’re not talking about marginal safety gains. The data represents a fundamental shift from harm reduction to harm prevention.
The methodology matters: I used their dynamic geographic benchmarks (comparing like-for-like road conditions) and verified the findings hold across San Francisco, Phoenix, LA, and Austin. The safety advantage actually increases in more complex urban environments.
Link to raw data below….
Notes on my approach:
Analysis based on 96 million miles of Waymo Rider-Only (RO) data through June 2025, utilizing Waymo's dynamic geographic benchmarks to compare Waymo Driver performance against human drivers under similar road conditions and operational design domains.
The projections for national impact (deaths prevented, societal costs) involve several assumptions. Given Waymo's zero reported fatalities, the direct serious injury reductions were mapped to national fatality statistics using established NHTSA-derived ratios that correlate serious injury crash rates with fatality rates. This extrapolation assumes that Waymo's observed serious injury prevention capability would translate proportionally to fatality prevention. Societal cost savings are estimated by applying average per-fatality and per-injury economic costs (e.g., medical, lost productivity, quality of life) as published by NHTSA, scaling these national averages to the projected number of avoided fatalities and injuries based on Waymo's safety performance. These figures represent the potential annual impact if the Waymo Driver's safety profile were widely integrated into the national fleet.

title: prinz (@deredleritt3r)
summary:
When opining on expected progress in reasoning models over the next few years, frontier lab employees will understandably discuss only publicly available models.
But here's where we stand on these metrics with unreleased models:
1. "Models will be able to autonomously work for full days (8 working hours) by mid-2026."
In fact, an unreleased OpenAI model that won second place in the Atcoder competition (July 2025) reasoned autonomously for 10 hours.
My guess is that OpenAI would not have had this model compete if they thought that the model has only a 10% or 20% chance of performing well. Yes, this means that it's possible that we're much farther ahead on the METR benchmark than most people realize.
2. "At least one model will match the performance of human experts across many industries before the end of 2026."
First, Sholto Douglas separately said that he expects a model to cross the 50% threshold in the GDPval benchmark (i.e., match human experts) later this year - presumably, for an Anthropic model.
Second, the GDPval paper unsurprisingly shows that increased reasoning effort produces stronger results on the benchmark. GPT-5 High scored 38.8%. How would GPT-5 Pro do? What about the unreleased reasoning model that got gold medals on the IMO, IOI and the ICPC? Does anyone really think that this model would fail to beat Claude Opus 4.1's score of 47.6%?
3. "By the end of 2027, models will frequently outperform experts on many tasks."
I wouldn't be surprised if this happened much sooner. Let's not forget, OpenAI's stated goal of building reasoning models with "capability to plan over very long horizons [i.e., longer than 5 hours] and actually able to retain memory".
Quoting @SmokeAwayyy

title: prinz (@deredleritt3r)
summary:
Sholto Douglas (Anthropic):
"Over the last year, RL has finally allow[ed] us to take a feedback loop and turn it into a model that is at least as good as the best humans at a given thing in a narrow domain. And you're seeing that with mathematics and competition code, which are the two domains most amendable to this - where rapidly the models are becoming incredibly competent competition mathematicians and competition coders.
There's nothing intrinsically different about competition code and math. It's just that they're really [more] amenable to RL than any other domain. But importantly, they demonstrate there's no intellectual ceiling on the models. They're capable of doing really tough reasoning given the right feedback loop. So, we think that same approach generalizes to basically all other domains of human intellectual endeavor where given the right feedback loop, these models will [become] at least as good as the best humans at a given thing. And then once you have something that is at least as good as the best humans at a thing, you can just run 1,000 of them in parallel or 100x faster and you have something that's even just with that condition substantially smarter than any given human. And this is completely throwing aside whether or not it's possible to make something that is smarter than a human.
The implications of this are pretty staggering, right? In the next 2 or 3 years given the right feedback loops, given the right compute, etc., we think that we as the AI industry as a whole on track to create something that is at least as capable as most humans on most computer-facing tasks possibly as good as many of our best scientists at their fields. It'll be sharp and spiky, there'll be examples of things it can't [do]. But the world will change.
... I think this is worth crying from the rooftops a little bit - guys, anything that we can measure seems to be improving really rapidly. Where does that get us in 2 or 3 years? I can't say for certain. But I think it's it's worth building into worldviews that there's a pretty serious chance that we get AGI."

summary:
August 2025: Oxford and Cambridge mathematicians publish a paper entitled "No LLM Solved Yu Tsumura's 554th Problem".
They gave this problem to o3 Pro, Gemini 2.5 Deep Think, Claude Opus 4 (Extended Thinking) and other models, with instructions to "not perform a web search to solve the problem". No LLM could solve it.
The paper smugly claims: "We show, contrary to the optimism about LLM’s problem-solving abilities, fueled by the recent gold medals that were attained, that a problem exists—Yu Tsumura’s 554th problem—that a) is within the scope of an IMO problem in terms of proof sophistication, b) is not a combinatorics problem which has caused issues for LLMs, c) requires fewer proof techniques than typical hard IMO problems, d) has a publicly available solution (likely in the training data of LLMs), and e) that cannot be readily solved by any existing off-the-shelf LLM (commercial or open-source)."
(Apparently, these mathematicians didn't get the memo that the unreleased OpenAI and Google models that won gold on the IMO are significantly more powerful than the publicly available models they tested. But no matter.)
October 2025: GPT-5 Pro solves Yu Tsumura's 554th problem in 15 minutes.
Lee Sedol moment is coming for many.
Quoting @nasqret
GPT-5-Pro solved, in just 15 minutes (without any internet search), the presentation problem known as “Yu Tsumura’s 554th Problem.”
This is the first model to solve this task completely. I expect more such results soon — the model demonstrates a strong grasp of elementary abstract algebra reasoning.

title: prinz (@deredleritt3r)
summary:
We are indeed at a crossroads with LLMs.
Where we are: GPT-5 Pro is able to generate minor novel advancements in math (but probably nothing a human expert wouldn't be able to generate). OpenAI's models can propose optimizations for its chips, but only of the kind human experts already had on their to-do list. Agentic coding tools work for many use cases, but, e.g., Andrej Karpathy found them unhelpful in creating nanochat "possibly [because] the repo is too far off the data distribution".
Where we could go (optimistic scenario): Better models finally enable Move 37 across many scientific disciplines; the world is never the same thereafter. I tend to think that we will see exactly this optimistic scenario materialize. For example, you may recall that Jascha Sohl-Dickstein wrote two weeks ago that "we're likely to see AI solving real open research problems in math in the next months".
Where we could also go (pessimistic scenario): It turns out that there is a ceiling on LLM intelligence that is roughly equivalent to the ceiling of extant human intelligence. Move 37 turns out to be impossible outside very narrow domains like Go. What then?
The answer, in my view, is that the world will still materially change. I look to my own profession for guidance on what we might see elsewhere. First, as knowledge regarding the capabilities of models like GPT-5 Pro diffuses (and as these models inevitably become cheaper), legal research will become the domain of AI, with a knowledgeable human in the loop. Second, solid agentic tools and harnesses for drafting legal briefs and agreements will inevitably be built (some companies are building them already). Third, we will have fine-tuned models capable of "writing like a lawyer"; these models will be able to suggest language for legal documents and client communications as proficiently as tools like autocomplete are able to generate basic text today. Fourth, enterprises will figure out, after some trial and error, how to stuff company-specific knowledge and preferences into context with great effect - which will greatly reduce friction between the generalist LLM and the need for company-specific output that the LLM must generate. These advances will completely change the legal profession - and many other professions - again, WITHOUT the need for more powerful AI models than those that exist today.
These, then, are our two possible futures: we are destined either for the stars or merely for very significant economic growth. Here's hoping for the former. Much will be revealed over the course of the next ~12 months.
Quoting @AndrewCurran_
We're in a strange spot right now with AI. The anti-AI crowd believes progress has halted and are doing a victory lap. Insiders at all labs maintain advancement continues at pace. Only one of these versions of reality will survive the new year. Gemini 3 is very close now.

Google and Yale scientists have trained an LLM that has generated a novel hypothesis about cancer cellular behavior. This prediction was confirmed multiple times in vitro.
- "What made this prediction so exciting was that it was a novel idea. Although CK2 has been implicated in many cellular functions, including as a modulator of the immune system, inhibiting CK2 via silmitasertib has not been reported in the literature to explicitly enhance MHC-I expression or antigen presentation. This highlights that the model was generating a new, testable hypothesis, and not just repeating known facts."
The model that generated this prediction is a 27B-parameter LLM based on the Google Gemma open source models, and trained on a corpus comprising >1B tokens of transcriptomic data, biological text, and metadata. Quite remarkable that a small (just 27B) LLM trained on specialized data is able to make novel scientific discoveries.

GPT-5 has been used to find solutions in existing literature to 10 Erdos problems that were previously considered unsolved.
Terence Tao, commenting on this:
"I am increasingly of the opinion that the most productive near-term adoptions of AI in mathematics will primarily come... from using medium-powered tools to accelerate and scale up more mundane and time-consuming, but still essential, research tasks, using the accumulated human experience... In such use cases, the output of the AI tool could also have been produced (with increased expenditure of time and attention) by a human expert - but this is actually a feature rather than a bug, as it allows for the AI output to be readily and reliably assessed, confirmed, and converted to a format that such experts are already comfortable working with.
An example of such a mundane task is literature review: locating relevant prior literature on a given problem."
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G3e163cXsAAGEOP.png
Quoting @MarkSellke
Update: Mehtaab and I pushed further on this. Using thousands of GPT5 queries, we found solutions to 10 Erdős problems that were listed as open: 223, 339, 494, 515, 621, 822, 883 (part 2/2), 903, 1043, 1079.
Additionally for 11 other problems, GPT5 found significant partial progress that we added to the official website: 32, 167, 188, 750, 788, 811, 827, 829, 1017, 1011, 1041. For 827, Erdős's original paper actually contained an error, and the work of Martínez and Roldán-Pensado explains this and fixes the argument.
The future of scientific research is going to be fun.

title: prinz (@deredleritt3r)
summary:
More details on Meta's new data center deal with Blue Owl, for those interested:
- Blue Owl Capital has created the SPV. The SPV will own an 80% interest in a joint venture (JV) with Meta; Meta will own the remaining 20%.
- The JV will own the landlord entity. The tenant will be owned by Meta.
- The data center owned by the landlord will initially (by June 1, 2029) be 2.064GW. As noted in my previous post, it has been reported that there are plans to eventually expand this to 5GW.
- Meta will contribute $5.76B to the JV. Blue Owl will contribute $23.03B. Total committed to build the data center campus is $28.79B.
- Blue Owl's commitment is funded via: (1) issuance of $27.3B in debt by the SPV; (2) $2.45B in equity; and (3) $1.16B in "interest income".
- The debt will mature in May 2049, which is the same as the end of Meta's lease obligations.
- The debt has been rated A+ by S&P, which is one notch lower than Meta's credit rating (AA-).
- An unusual feature of the debt is that there is no direct asset pledge - i.e., the creditors have no recourse on the data center assets in case of non-payment.
- Meta tenant's rent payment obligations start on June 1, 2029. Meta tenant is required to pay the rent in full even if there are construction delays (except that certain limited rent abatements and rent credits are available due to delays resulting from force majeure and landlord's failure to pay contractors).
- Meta tenant pays rent based on a 50% data center utilization rate for the first 19 months, and based on the actual utilization rate thereafter. Meta tenant ALSO reimburses all operating costs and maintenance costs. The rent schedule has a minimum rent level, even if the project isn't utilized. "Unlike other data center leases, this project’s lease doesn’t contain any key performance indicators (KPIs), the failure of which would result in rent abatements or potential termination of lease."
- Meta provides a payment guaranty for Meta tenant's rent and operating expenses obligations.
- Meta and Entergy Louisiana LLC have entered into an electric service agreement ending November 30, 2041, with an automatic 5-year renewal. Entergy is required to provide up to 3GW of power to the campus by December 2028 (i.e., 6 months before the rent start date). “This is subject to completing one new substation, two major transmission lines, three power generation plants, and acquiring 860 MW of generation capacity." The total project construction cost includes Meta's contribution to support the construction of these generation capacities.
- The lease term is 4 years, and it subsequently renews for four further 4-year periods (20 years total).
- Meta cannot terminate the lease, except: (1) on account of condemnation; or (2) only during operations phase, on account of a casualty event that can't be repaired within 24 months (which has an occurrence probability of 0.01% - 0.10%).
- Meta provides a unique Residual Value Guarantee (RVG), which is intended to be sufficient to cover outstanding debt at the end of each 4-year lease term. Under this RVG, Meta is required to pay a guaranteed minimum value to the SPV if: (1) Meta exits the leases after any 4-year term before the full debt repayment; or (2) there has been a Meta tenant default or bankruptcy.

Task length is important, because it unlocks the ability for a human to supervise a team of models, each of which works autonomously for hours at a time (vs. having to having to talk to an agent every 10 minutes to give it feedback).
- "Extremely likely" that the current approach to training AI models (pre-training, RL) is going to produce a system that can perform at roughly human level in basically all tasks we care about productivity-wise.

AI is "absolutely discovering novel things" already, and "we're just moving up the scale of how impressive, how interesting are the things it is able to discover on its own."
- "Highly likely" that sometime next year we're going to have some discoveries that people unanimously agree are super-impressive.
- AI will be able to on its own make a breakthrough that is worthy of a Nobel Prize in 2027 or 2028.

Two highlights for me in the changes to OpenAI's agreement with Microsoft:

Quoting @AndrewCurran_
OpenAI has completed its recapitalization. The nonprofit is now called the OpenAI Foundation. Big changes to the relationship between OpenAI and Microsoft. We finally get to see the ownership numbers. I will quote:
'Microsoft holds an investment in OpenAI Group PBC valued at approximately $135 billion, representing roughly 27 percent on an as-converted diluted basis, inclusive of all owners—employees, investors, and the OpenAI Foundation. Excluding the impact of OpenAI’s recent funding rounds, Microsoft held a 32.5 percent stake on an as-converted basis in the OpenAI for-profit.'
Full list of changes:
- Once AGI is declared by OpenAI, that declaration will now be verified by an independent expert panel.
- Microsoft’s IP rights for both models and products are extended through 2032 and now includes models post-AGI, with appropriate safety guardrails.
- Microsoft’s IP rights to research, defined as the confidential methods used in the development of models and systems, will remain until either the expert panel verifies AGI or through 2030, whichever is first. Research IP includes, for example, models intended for internal deployment or research only. Beyond that, research IP does not include model architecture, model weights, inference code, finetuning code, and any IP related to data center hardware and software; and Microsoft retains these non-Research IP rights.
- Microsoft’s IP rights now exclude OpenAI’s consumer hardware.
- OpenAI can now jointly develop some products with third parties. API products developed with third parties will be exclusive to Azure. Non-API products may be served on any cloud provider.
Microsoft can now independently pursue AGI alone or in partnership with third parties.
- The revenue share agreement remains until the expert panel verifies AGI, though payments will be made over a longer period of time.
- OpenAI has contracted to purchase an incremental $250B of Azure services, and Microsoft will no longer have a right of first refusal to be OpenAI’s compute provider.
OpenAI can now provide API access to US government national security customers, regardless of the cloud provider.
- OpenAI is now able to release open weight models that meet requisite capability criteria.

title: prinz (@deredleritt3r)
summary:
Yesterday, I had a question come up at work about mailing addresses and Emplyer Identification Numbers (FEINs) of 6 different subsidiaries of a certain public company. This information isn't typically onerous to obtain (it's usually in a data room somewhere or an e-mail/phone call away), but this time I decided to use GPT-5 Pro to find it instead.
Prompt: "Please find FEINs and addresses for the following companies: [names]. Use high-quality sources only."
I expected that GPT-5 Pro would work for ~15 minutes and return almost no hits. FEINs in particular are nearly impossible to find for random subs of a big company. But to my surprise, GPT-5 Pro worked for >45 minutes AND gave me good results.
- For 4 companies out of 6, GPT-5 Pro found FEINs hidden away on the Florida Division of Corporations' website. These are not Florida companies, but they operate in Florida, which presumably requires them to register with the Florida Division of Corporations. I had no idea previously that Florida publishes FEINs on its website, and would never have thought to look there. All FEINs were correct (I double-checked them).
BTW, searching the Florida website requires entering the company's name in a search box and clicking on the "search" button. These search results are not indexed by Google (I checked this morning). Is GPT-5 Pro now able to fill out forms and click on buttons (like ChatGPT Agent)?
- GPT-5 Pro also found an address for 1 of the 6 companies by checking FINRA BrokerCheck records of a subsidiary of this company. In the lengthy BrokerCheck PDF report, there are fields for names and addresses of the registrant's parent companies. One of the parent companies was a company I was looking for. Again, I never would have found this on my own; I didn't even know that one of the companies I was searching for had a subsidiary registered with FINRA.
This search was very compute-intensive and took a long time, but ofc that's okay because I can do other work while GPT-5 Pro runs in the background and because the billable time for an associate to find this information would have been more expensive regardless. More and more, I have been finding that just about any search query that would take me more than a few seconds to process is much better routed through GPT-5 than Google search.
Quoting @deredleritt3r
@jcsemantics I beat my personal record today: 45 m 48 s
Domain: finding some obscure publicly available information for each of 6 subsidiaries of a public company.

title: prinz (@deredleritt3r)
summary:
1. OpenAI expects to end the year at a $20B annualized revenue run rate.
2. There is an "upcoming enterprise offering".
3. "Given everything we see on the horizon in our research program, this is the time to invest to be really scaling up our technology [i.e., data center infrastructure]."
4. A world where AI can make important scientific breakthroughs at the cost of tremendous amounts of computing power is something OpenAI "no longer think[s] is in the distant future".
Quoting @sama
I would like to clarify a few things.
First, the obvious one: we do not have or want government guarantees for OpenAI datacenters. We believe that governments should not pick winners or losers, and that taxpayers should not bail out companies that make bad business decisions or otherwise lose in the market. If one company fails, other companies will do good work.
What we do think might make sense is governments building (and owning) their own AI infrastructure, but then the upside of that should flow to the government as well. We can imagine a world where governments decide to offtake a lot of computing power and get to decide how to use it, and it may make sense to provide lower cost of capital to do so. Building a strategic national reserve of computing power makes a lot of sense. But this should be for the government’s benefit, not the benefit of private companies.
The one area where we have discussed loan guarantees is as part of supporting the buildout of semiconductor fabs in the US, where we and other companies have responded to the government’s call and where we would be happy to help (though we did not formally apply). The basic idea there has been ensuring that the sourcing of the chip supply chain is as American as possible in order to bring jobs and industrialization back to the US, and to enhance the strategic position of the US with an independent supply chain, for the benefit of all American companies. This is of course different from governments guaranteeing private-benefit datacenter buildouts.
There are at least 3 “questions behind the question” here that are understandably causing concern.
First, “How is OpenAI going to pay for all this infrastructure it is signing up for?” We expect to end this year above $20 billion in annualized revenue run rate and grow to hundreds of billion by 2030. We are looking at commitments of about $1.4 trillion over the next 8 years. Obviously this requires continued revenue growth, and each doubling is a lot of work! But we are feeling good about our prospects there; we are quite excited about our upcoming enterprise offering for example, and there are categories like new consumer devices and robotics that we also expect to be very significant. But there are also new categories we have a hard time putting specifics on like AI that can do scientific discovery, which we will touch on later.
We are also looking at ways to more directly sell compute capacity to other companies (and people); we are pretty sure the world is going to need a lot of “AI cloud”, and we are excited to offer this. We may also raise more equity or debt capital in the future.
But everything we currently see suggests that the world is going to need a great deal more computing power than what we are already planning for.
Second, “Is OpenAI trying to become too big to fail, and should the government pick winners and losers?” Our answer on this is an unequivocal no. If we screw up and can’t fix it, we should fail, and other companies will continue on doing good work and servicing customers. That’s how capitalism works and the ecosystem and economy would be fine. We plan to be a wildly successful company, but if we get it wrong, that’s on us.
Our CFO talked about government financing yesterday, and then later clarified her point underscoring that she could have phrased things more clearly. As mentioned above, we think that the US government should have a national strategy for its own AI infrastructure.
Tyler Cowen asked me a few weeks ago about the federal government becoming the insurer of last resort for AI, in the sense of risks (like nuclear power) not about overbuild. I said “I do think the government ends up as the insurer of last resort, but I think I mean that in a different way than you mean that, and I don’t expect them to actually be writing the policies in the way that maybe they do for nuclear”. Again, this was in a totally different context than datacenter buildout, and not about bailing out a company. What we were talking about is something going catastrophically wrong—say, a rogue actor using an AI to coordinate a large-scale cyberattack that disrupts critical infrastructure—and how intentional misuse of AI could cause harm at a scale that only the government could deal with. I do not think the government should be writing insurance policies for AI companies.
Third, “Why do you need to spend so much now, instead of growing more slowly?”. We are trying to build the infrastructure for a future economy powered by AI, and given everything we see on the horizon in our research program, this is the time to invest to be really scaling up our technology. Massive infrastructure projects take quite awhile to build, so we have to start now.
Based on the trends we are seeing of how people are using AI and how much of it they would like to use, we believe the risk to OpenAI of not having enough computing power is more significant and more likely than the risk of having too much. Even today, we and others have to rate limit our products and not offer new features and models because we face such a severe compute constraint.
In a world where AI can make important scientific breakthroughs but at the cost of tremendous amounts of computing power, we want to be ready to meet that moment. And we no longer think it’s in the distant future. Our mission requires us to do what we can to not wait many more years to apply AI to hard problems, like contributing to curing deadly diseases, and to bring the benefits of AGI to people as soon as possible.
Also, we want a world of abundant and cheap AI. We expect massive demand for this technology, and for it to improve people’s lives in many ways.
It is a great privilege to get to be in the arena, and to have the conviction to take a run at building infrastructure at such scale for something so important. This is the bet we are making, and given our vantage point, we feel good about it. But we of course could be wrong, and the market—not the government—will deal with it if we are.

summary:
My AI investment thesis is "feel the AGI" - i.e., the entire economy will benefit.
Quoting @yishan
My AI investment thesis is that every AI application startup is likely to be crushed by rapid expansion of the foundational model providers.
App functionality will be added to the foundational models' offerings, because the big players aren't slow incumbents (it is wrong to apply the analogy of "fast startup, slow incumbent" here), they are just big. Far more so than with any other prior new technology, there is a massive and fast-moving wave that obsoletes every new app almost as fast as it can be invented. There is almost no time to build a company and scale it.
There are two ways AI application startup founders can make money:
- Make a flash-in-the-pan app that generates a ton of cash and bank the cash (my estimate is that you have about 12-18 months cashflow generation)
- Make a good enough app that you get acquired by one of the big players for sufficient equity
The situation is highly unstable - we don't know if it's going to crash or go to the moon but both scenarios make it very unlikely that any AI application startup will independently become a generational supercompany (baseline odds are low to begin with).
The best odds are finding an application niche in a highly specialized field with extremely unique and specific data barriers, ideally ones relating to real atoms (hardware or world-related) data and not software/finance.

title: prinz (@deredleritt3r)
summary:
Only two evals matter now:
1. How useful is this model for automating white-collar work?
2. Can this model discover novel science?
Note that neither of these evals can be reduced to a nice little bar chart at model release. It usually takes (at least) a few months of real-world use to get a feeling for a model's abilities vis-a-vis these evals.
OpenAI hit a home run with GPT-5 on eval 1, which was obvious from the start, but took the timeline a full 3 months to grok. Mark my words: GPT-5.1 is a big step in the same direction.
Eval 2 requires either a giga-expensive model that thinks for many hours at a time (which you won't get with a consumer-grade model) or a model that is particularly well-suited for multi-agent systems like Google's AI Co-Scientist (which my gut feeling tells me is probably a model that also scores well on eval 1 - but let's wait and see).
All other popular evals are mostly holdovers from the time when LLMs were toys suitable for general consumer use, but not for any serious real-world applications. We're now far past that stage. Time to let go of the charts with pretty bar lines and model rankings and start actually using the models for your productive use cases.
Quoting @sandersted
@kimmonismus short answer is:
- GPT-5.1 evals are fairly similar
- evals are pretty irrelevant to most usage (very few people are doing math proofs with ChatGPT)
- felt we’d rather keep working on making better AIs than halt for a week or two to prep a giant comprehensive hypey blog post

title: prinz (@deredleritt3r)
summary:
Microsoft does have rights to all of OpenAI's IP (excluding consumer hardware), BUT:
- For most IP, these rights extend only through 2032. This category includes, e.g., model architecture, model weights, inference code, finetuning code, and any IP related to data center hardware and software.
- For "research IP", these rights extend only through the earlier of: (a) 2030; or (b) declaration of AGI verified by independent panel. This includes "confidential methods used in the development of models and systems", such as models intended for internal deployment or research only.
- Most importantly, Microsoft cannot use OpenAI's IP to develop AGI except to develop models under certain specified compute thresholds, which are "significantly larger than the size of systems used to train leading models today". This clause expires when OpenAI's declaration of AGI is verified by an independent panel.
Thus, assuming that AGI winds up being a gigantic model (probably a good assumption), Microsoft won't be able to do much to develop its own AGI until after OpenAI has already declared AGI. At that point, Microsoft will have a copy of the AGI model's weights and will be able to directly race against OpenAI to develop even better models ("ASI"). OpenAI won't have to share its own "ASI" models with Microsoft, so long as they're models used only for "internal deployment" or "research".

For a better read of the true capabilities of OpenAI's models in July (4 months ago, for those counting), consider the unreleased model that placed second in the Atcoder competition. It placed second in the competition; only one insanely cracked human beat it.
The next leap in professional-grade AI models is models that are capable of making small novel scientific discoveries. I trust that we'll be hearing from OpenAI (and probably others) on that front fairly soon.

title: prinz (@deredleritt3r)
summary:
The most important insight about AI, distilled into one sentence:
"[GenAI is] trained to model the *entire distribution*, and RL lets it go beyond the human distribution."
Quoting @polynoamial
The biggest misconception I hear about GenAI is that it inevitably outputs slop because it's trained to output "the average of the internet". But that's simply not true. It's trained to model the *entire distribution*, and RL lets it go beyond the human distribution.
AlphaGo was a perfect demonstration of this. It learned the human distribution by training on a lot of Go games. Then, it used RL to go beyond the human distribution by discovering Move 37, a brilliant move that human experts initially thought was a blunder.
AlphaGo was a narrow domain with an infinite curriculum and a perfect reward signal. The real world is a lot harder, and the jagged frontier of AI intelligence hasn't really surpassed top human capabilities yet.
But we're already starting to see LLMs contribute meaningfully to scientific research. As pretraining, RL, and test-time compute are scaled further, I expect we'll soon see a Move 37 for science.

Why insurance companies are looking to exclude AI-related incidents from their liability policies:
- An insurance company will happily cover just about any risk that its underwriters can price, BUT...

Ilya Sutskever on the mountain he's climbing with SSI:
1. Dwarkesh and Ilya discuss how easy it is for a teenager to learn how to drive - takes 10 hours.
Ilya: "People exhibit great reliability, robustness, and ability to learn in a domain that did not exist until recently [like driving cars]" - which seems to indicate that people have "just better machine learning, period". This is because humans have a "very robust" value function: a teenager learning to drive immediately has the sense of how well or badly he/she is doing, how confident or unconfident he/she is.
Dwarkesh asks: So, how do we reconceptualize the way we're training models to make this type of learning possible?
Ilya answers: "It's a question I have a lot of opinions about. But unfortunately, we live in a world where not all machine learning ideas are discussed freely, and this is one of them."
This is clearly a direction SSI is actively working on, and he's not at liberty to disclose anything else.
2. Ilya says that OpenAI's definition of "AGI" (outperforming most humans at most economically valuable work) has overshot what we need. The goal is to produce a superintelligent AI that learns in the world after it is deployed:

Here is how DeepSeek-V3.2-Speciale stacks up against OpenAI and Google in IMO, IOI and ICPC performance:
1. Speciale adhered to each competition's time and attempt limits. No tools or internet access were used.
2. For the IOI and ICPC, OpenAI had GPT-5 generate candidate solutions. The unreleased experimental model reviewed these solutions and decided which were to be submitted. For the hardest ICPC problem, the unreleased experimental model generated the solution on its own.
DeepSeek used a much more complex 3-stage process for Speciale:
(1) First, solutions that exceeded "the length constraints" or "failed to pass the provided sample cases" (no idea what this means) were eliminated.
(2) Second, a DeepSeek-V32-Exp model was used to remove solutions in which Speciale refused, or indicated that it was unable to, solve the problem.
(3) Third, the solution(s) with the longest thinking traces were selected for final submission.
I am especially curious what it means that solutions which "failed to pass the provided sample cases" were eliminated. What were the "sample cases" provided to the model?
3. IMO performance: Speciale solved 5 problems out of 6 (same as OpenAI and Google).
4. IOI performance: Speciale got 492/600 (10th), lagging behind OpenAI's performance of 533.29/600 (6th).
5. ICPC performance: Speciale solved 10 problems out of 12, same as Google - but lagging behind OpenAI's performance of 12/12.
Congrats to the DeepSeek team!

New interview with Mark Chen (OpenAI):
- Ashlee Vance, the interviewer, has apparently been spending a lot of time at OpenAI, including sitting in on meetings (he seems to be writing a book). And he seems to think that OpenAI has made some huge advance in pre-training: "Pre-training seems like this area where it seems is you've figured something out, you're excited about. You think this is going to be a major advance."
Mark doesn't spill the beans, though. He does say: "We think there's a lot of room in pre-training. A lot of people say scaling is dead. We don't think so at all."
And also this: "We absolutely want to keep scaling the models and we have algorithmic breakthroughs that enable us to scale the models." Mark also mentions that OpenAI has "strong algorithms" around data efficiency.
- Finally more clarity on the automated AI researcher:
"Within a year, we want to change the nature of the way that we're doing research. We want to be productively relying on AI interns in the research development process. And within 2.5 years, we want AI to be doing end-to-end research. Today, you come up with an idea, you execute on it, you implement it, you debug it. Within a year, we're quite confident we can get to a world where we control the outer loop - we come up with the ideas, but the model is in charge of the implementation and debugging."
- On memory and the Jony Ive device:
"ChatGPT feels very dumb to me - it doesn't feel very thinking-native. If you go to it with a prompt, you get a response, and then it's doing no productive work for you until you give it the next prompt. And if you give it a similar prompt, it's going to think for the same amount of time; it hasn't gotten smarter because you asked the first prompt. The future is going to be a world where memory will be an improved feature. Every time you go to ChatGPT, it learns something deep about you. It reflects about why you would ask this question, related questions, anything. And then the next time you go to it, it's going to be much smarter. And that begs the question of how do you design a device that has this as the dominating thesis."
Also, Mark "may or may not" have a prototype of the device already.
- On OpenAI's portfolio of big bets, including synthetic data:
Mark says that OpenAI is scaling up several big bets aggressively, including one around synthetic data that was mentioned around the GPT-5 launch.
For those curious what this means, Sebastian Bubeck made a short cameo during the GPT-5 launch wherein he mentioned "new training techniques" whereby o3 generated synthetic data to train GPT-5 in a way "raw web data just never could". The point was to generate not a large volume of data cheaply, but rather useful training data. "This interaction between models foreshadows a recursive self-improvement loop."

FAP is a rare, inherited colorectal cancer predisposition disease with no approved medicines. Shane Legg, Google:

Also, 50% chance of achieving "mini-AGI" by 2028 - i.e., an AI that can carry out all the kinds of cognitive tasks that a human can do, without failing in ways that surprise us.

Quoting @Hangsiin
Shane Legg(@ShaneLegg), the cofounder of Google DeepMind, discussed the definition of AGI, its timeline, and its socio economic impact.
1.
-Today’s AI has made a lot of progress compared with five years ago, but it still has many weaknesses and is uneven.
-Among its weaknesses, the most salient are continual learning and visual reasoning.
-However, I do not think there are any fundamental obstacles here, and we have ideas about how to build systems that can do these things.
-So I think all of these problems will be solved within a few years.
2.
-When artificial agents can at least carry out all the kinds of cognitive tasks that we would typically expect a human to be able to do, I call that “minimum AGI.”
-It could take one year or it could take five, but my current guess is around two years.
-That is the point where we can say, “Okay, when we give this AI cognitive tasks the way we would give them to a person, it no longer fails in ways that would surprise us.”
3.
-I think the transition from “full AGI” to ASI will definitely happen.
-Human intelligence will not be the upper bound, and based on compute we will see AIs vastly surpass human intelligence.
4.
-Over the next few years, AI systems will shift from being very useful tools to doing more and more work that is directly economically valuable.
-This process will be uneven. For example, in software engineering you might go from needing 100 people to needing 20 people a few years from now, and those 20 will be using advanced AI tools.
-That will cause some disruption in labor markets in certain areas, and as that happens I think the discussion around AI will become much more serious.
-Jobs like plumbing may be more protected from being replaced by AI.
-The work that is actually at risk is the “elite cognitive labor” that is currently very highly rewarded, including top lawyers, AI researchers, software engineers, and some mathematicians.
-If your job can be done remotely over the internet using only a laptop, then a powerful AI running on that same substrate will be able to do it instead.
-Many sociologists and economists still do not take AGI seriously, but a year from now things will look much clearer than they do today. They are not yet seeing the trend.
5.
-50 percent chance of reaching “minimum AGI” by 2028 (he is sticking to his 2008 prediction).
-“Full AGI” will come a few years after “minimum AGI” (about 3, 4, 5 or 6 years later), and he is confident it will definitely happen within 10 years.

My 2c on this debate:
I have a hard time understanding how a model that, when equipped with some additional harnesses and connectivities, could probably successfully substitute for a junior associate at a law firm (at most tasks that junior associates actually do) does not qualify as "AGI".*
This should be slowly coming into view for anyone who has used GPT-5.x Pro for legal research and analysis.
* defined as OpenAI does (did?) in its agreement with Microsoft: an autonomous system that outperforms humans at most economically valuable work
Quoting @deanwball
I agree with all this; it is why I also believe that opus 4.5 in claude code is basically AGI.
Most people barely noticed, but *it is happening.*
It’s just happening, at first, in a conceptually weird way: Anyone can now, with quite high reliability and reasonable assurances of quality, cause bespoke software engineering to occur.
This is a strange concept. Most people, going about their day, do not think about how "causing bespoke software engineering to occur" might improve their lives or allow them to achieve some objective. They think of "software engineering," when they think of it at all, as something altogether distinct from what they do. Of course if you have deeply internalized the general-purpose nature of "software," and especially, "things achievable by well-orchestrated computers," you understand that in some important sense, almost all human endeavor can be aided, in some way or another, by software engineering. A great deal of it can be automated altogether.
Coding agents have reached the point of reliability and quality where it is now possible to cause a great many moderately complex software engineering projects to occur. I would not quite say "automate," both because it is not in fact automatic (the human has to remain at least kind of engaged throughout the process; even "vibe coding" is a form of engagement) and because "automate" implies a "set it and forget it" mentality that is not at all consonant with what these coding agents require of their human users.
You have seen the threads on X with mind-exploding emojis. You have seen the LinkedIn-style "everyone is a software engineer now" content. You have perhaps seen thoughtful reflective essays on Substack and personal blogs. It has been talked about before incessantly, often in much too hype-y a manner. It has been talked about so much that you would not be mistaken to roll your eyes, because the predictions have not quite panned out. Even today, the methods I have gestured at in this essay do not work perfectly.
Yet it is happening nonetheless.
The potential is shockingly vast if you have conceptualized these tools appropriately (remember, for instance, that a large language model is itself a software tool, accessible through an application programming interface by your coding agents to accomplish all of the things a software engineer can use a large language model to accomplish).
It will take time to realize this potential, if for no other reason than the fact that for most people, the tool I am describing and the mentality required to wield it well are entirely alien. You have to learn to think a little bit like a software engineer; you have to know "the kinds of things software can do." You have to learn also to think like the chief executive of a thousand small (but fast growing) teams of software engineers who possess expert-level knowledge of virtually all domains of human intellectual life. Grasping all of this, and learning how to embody it, requires humans to adopt a strange and new kind of agenticness. Not all of us will.
But some people understand it already, and their numbers will only grow. Young people in particular, blessed with neuroplasticity, will have internalized this to a depth few grownups will be able to comprehend. This transformation will therefore be sociological as well as technological, the revolution cultural as well as industrial.
We lack “transformative AI” only because it is hard to recognize transformation *while it is in its early stages.* But the transformation is underway. Technical and infrastructural advancements will make it easier to use and better able to learn new skills. It will, of course, get smarter.
Diffusion will proceed slower than you’d like but faster than you’d think. New institutions, built with AI-contingent assumptions from the ground up, will be born.
So don’t listen to the chatterers. Watch, instead, what is happening.

summary:
OpenAI's Preparedness Framework was updated in April 2025 to include AI self-improvement capabilities as one of the three Tracked Categories.
Tracked Categories are those that are: (1) plausible, (2) measurable, (3) severe, (4) net new, and (5) instantaneous/irremediable (see definitions in the screenshot below). Most interestingly, "plausible" means that it is "possible to identify a causal pathway for a severe harm in the capability area, enabled by frontier AI".
Per OpenAI, self-improvement became a Tracked Category in April 2025 because "it presents a distinct plausible, net new, and potentially irremediable risk, namely that of a hard-to-track rapid acceleration in AI capabilities which could have hard-to-predict severely harmful consequences".
In contrast, things like "long-range autonomy" and "autonomous replication and adaptation" are currently designated merely as Research Categories by OpenAI - i.e., they do not (yet) qualify as Tracked Categories.
One might ask what it is about AI self-improvement that made OpenAI designate it as "plausible" in April.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G9Nlr-kWoAA0HNA.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G9Nlxv9WsAA17LM.jpg
Quoting @sama
We are hiring a Head of Preparedness. This is a critical role at an important time; models are improving quickly and are now capable of many great things, but they are also starting to present some real challenges. The potential impact of models on mental health was something we saw a preview of in 2025; we are just now seeing models get so good at computer security they are beginning to find critical vulnerabilities.
We have a strong foundation of measuring growing capabilities, but we are entering a world where we need more nuanced understanding and measurement of how those capabilities could be abused, and how we can limit those downsides both in our products and in the world, in a way that lets us all enjoy the tremendous benefits. These questions are hard and there is little precedent; a lot of ideas that sound good have some real edge cases.
If you want to help the world figure out how to enable cybersecurity defenders with cutting edge capabilities while ensuring attackers can't use them for harm, ideally by making all systems more secure, and similarly for how we release biological capabilities and even gain confidence in the safety of running systems that can self-improve, please consider applying.

title: prinz (@deredleritt3r)
summary:
In 1994, Jeff and MacKenzie Bezos moved to Bellevue, WA with a dream: to build a website to sell books online.
The website launched in July 1995. In the very first week, the new online bookstore called "Amazon" received $12,000 worth of orders. Because Amazon had no warehouse, each book ordered online had to be purchased by Amazon from a distributor, manually repackaged, and shipped to the customer.
Business grew quickly. By 1996, Amazon had $16M in annual revenue and had raised funds at a $60M valuation. By 1997, Amazon was offering more than 2.5M book titles on its website, "including most of the estimated 1.5M books believed to be in print", and had also made a brave jump into other product lines (CDs! Videotapes! Cassette tapes!). The website had a jaw-dropping 80,000 daily visits (up from 2,200 in just 15 months).
However fast Amazon grew, it was never enough for Bezos. In March 1997, Amazon went public at $18/share, equating to a ~$430M market cap. By the end of the first day of trading, its share price was up 31% to $23.50 (~$560M market cap).
By June 1998, Amazon's stock price had climbed to $75. The company planned to lose $1 per share in 1998 and $0.50 per share in 1999 before turning a profit in 2000. Analysts were incredulous:
"It's hard for me to understand why Amazon is worth 50% more than Barnes & Noble. Amazon has no earnings and just a Web site, while Barnes & Noble has earnings, a lot of bookstores and a smaller, but growing, Web site." - Hugh Lamle, executive VP at M.D. Sass Investors Services (June 22, 1998).
As the dot-com bubble grew, calls that Amazon was a scam, actually, grew louder. In May 1999, Barrons ran a hit piece called "Amazon.bomb", which caused Amazon's stock to tank by more than 20%. "Despite all the hoopla surrounding Amazon, Bezos has not really revolutionized the book industry at all," the article claimed, "he is a middleman, and he will likely be outflanked by companies that sell their wares directly to consumers... Publishing houses themselves could sell their books online. And new technologies promise to cut costs even further by allowing consumers to download books via the internet. Books can be printed out on traditional computer printers or put into a new notebook-sized computer device that displays books on its screen a page at a time... [And] what's to stop famous authors from establishing their own Websites to sell their books?"
No matter. After floundering for a bit, Amazon recovered. By December 1999, Amazon had a ~$36B market cap, up well over 70x(!) since its March 1997 IPO.
...and then, the dot-com bubble burst. This is the story with which most readers will already be familiar. Tough times followed for Amazon investors. After the events of September 11, 2001, Amazon was trading at a market cap under $3B, down over 90% from its peak dot-com-bubble valuation.
Today, with full benefits of hindsight, we can finally answer the question posed by sensationalist news media in the late 1990s: Was Amazon's price inflated, overvalued, a product of the dot-com craze, a fashionable--but poorly thought out--business model shilled by the hype merchant Jeff Bezos?
Let's find out. Earlier today, $AMZN closed at $246.29 per share, equating to a market cap of $2.63T. Thus, an investor "duped" by Jeff Bezos into buying the stock at the very height of the dot-com bubble (at a $36B valuation) and holding it through today's date would be up >50x in total, having earned a >15% average annual return.
This leads us to a startling conclusion. Much has been written in the news and on social media about the dot-com bubble and the "hype" surrounding it. But in truth, the best companies of the 1990s dot-com era - like Amazon - were never in a "bubble" at all! On the contrary, these companies had real business models that wound up generating very significant real value. Barrons was wrong. The analysts were wrong. Buying $AMZN in the 1990s was a great idea.
Indeed, the REAL take-away from the dot-com bubble is that hype surrounding genuinely good companies - like Amazon - often results in investors chasing "the next Amazon" and betting on poorly run companies in the same niche. In February 2000, Pets-dot-com raised $82.5M in its IPO. Alas, the company failed to generate revenue, and, just nine months later, it was bankrupt. (Ironically, Amazon was a significant investor in Pets-dot-com and lost a lot of money on this bet!)
The lesson we learn from all this about the "AI bubble" is not - as Terry Tao suggests below - that the AI companies "rely on hype" and will therefore crash and burn (resulting in "a more realistic equilibrium"), but rather that it should not surprise us if these companies survive and eventually thrive even if the "AI bubble" bursts - much like Amazon did.
The key, however, is not to be lured into investing in the "Pets-dot-com" of AI.
Quoting @haider1
Terence Tao says the current business model of big AI companies relies on hype to justify their massive valuations
The situation is similar to the dot-com boom, where the tech was real, but the early promises were inflated
"hopefully we'll reach a more realistic equilibrium in a year or two"

Give me ability to tell it to look at three precedent deals and put together a shell of a similar document (or import my own precedent). Give me ability to tell it to propose tweaks to Section X to do Y, or to revise provisions throughout the document to do Z. When this micro-task is done, give me a separate window with a redline of what it proposes to do, so that I could view, accept, reject, edit. Let it work on multiple micro-tasks at once. Give it the ability to search for publicly available info and propose certain changes on its own ("I found a regulatory issue; let me flag that for the user and propose some edits."). Give it the ability to connect to a data room for the project (if the data room provider allows) and do the same thing. Give it a nice way to search for precedent for a provision - click of a button and it finds a few and tells me where the language is from. Give it the skill to produce nice signature pages. Let it pick up edits that come to my mailbox (e-mails) from my team members and the client and have it work in the background on a parallel version of the agreement to implement them, all subject to my approval as a micro-task.
2. Give me another AI agent that is a "junior associate with access to e-mail". Whenever a client e-mails me some random changes to a doc or a research question, have it automatically pick it up in the background and start working. Do the research. Implement the annoying e-mail comments into the actual document (or ask the other agent mentioned above to implement them). Update our project checklist based on this new info. Give me a somewhat conspicuous alert that the work is done and awaiting my approval. Also, let me easily e-mail the agent with things that I want done while I'm away from my laptop.
As to Claude Cowork, I personally am very excited about its ability to search my local files, which seems to come with a nice UI. Yes, I know that Claude Code can do that too, but the percentage of lawyers who will be comfortable with using a CLI is probably <1%. And so, nice UI is critical. Nice UIs will (eventually) win over us non-technical people.
I'm really excited to see where this all takes us over the next 12 months.

title: prinz (@deredleritt3r)
summary:
And now for something completely different. Introducing: prinzbench.
Over the past few months, I have been increasingly using LLMs for legal work, primarily legal research and "needle-in-the-haystack" search queries. This is economically valuable work of the kind performed by many lawyers on a daily basis. It is also quite distinct from the benchmarks that the frontier labs typically "hill-climb" - i.e., math and coding. And importantly, correct legal analysis is not easily verifiable. There is no code to compile, there is no mathematical proof that either works or doesn't. The only way to know whether one reached the correct legal conclusion is to be confident that: (1) no legal authorities were missed when analyzing the question; and (2) the logical analysis of the relevant legal authorities was correct.
prinzbench is a private benchmark that aims to test LLMs' abilities to do exactly this kind of work: search the internet for relevant information and appropriately analyze it to form the correct legal conclusion.
The benchmark comprises 33 questions (25 Legal Research and 8 Search). Each model's response to a question was graded by me personally (without use of AI in grading) at pass@1. For each model, the complete benchmark was run 3 times, for a maximum score of 99 (33 questions * 3).
These 33 questions are hard! I intentionally picked difficult questions from my (quite niche) area of the law for the benchmark, and ad-hoc tested them against various LLMs before deciding whether to include each particular question in prinzbench. Many (already quite hard) questions were filtered out this way. The LLMs are becoming VERY good at very basic legal research, and the world seems to have barely noticed!
TL;DR on the results (and more details in the Readme linked below):
- GPT-5.2 Thinking is by far the best model out of those I tested, and the only model to (barely) get >50% of the questions right.
- The two Gemini 3 models are essentially tied for second place. They are very solid.
- The latest Grok models and Kimi K2-Thinking offer approximately the same (rather poor) performance on the benchmark.
- The biggest surprise for me was that Sonnet 4.5 and Opus 4.5 ranked dead last on the benchmark, with Sonnet handily beating Opus. These models are *awful* at the Search portion of the benchmark, each scoring 0/24 points. Sonnet's performance on the Legal Research portion of the benchmark was roughly the same as that of Grok/Kimi. Sonnet 4.5 seems to be a better legal reasoner than Opus 4.5.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G_MSM1sXwAECSYu.png
